summary: This document updates the syntax of Certificate Management Protocol version 2 and its HTTP transfer. It changes how encrypted values are carried by using EnvelopedData instead of EncryptedValue, clarifies p10cr messages, improves crypto agility, and adds general message types, extended key usages, and well-known URIs. It also introduces CMP version 3. It updates RFCs 4210, 5912, and 6712 and was later replaced by RFC 9810 and RFC 9811.

eli5.summary: A certificate-office rulebook needed fixes and new forms. This note lists them. Later, it was replaced by newer notes.

subtitle: Modernizing certificate management protocol with better encryption and flexibility.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) version 2, originally defined in 1999, uses EncryptedValue for protecting sensitive data. This structure is deprecated in newer cryptographic standards. CMP also lacks role-based extended key usages, flexible general message types, and other features needed for modern deployments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9480 updates CMP syntax to prefer EnvelopedData (a standard CMS structure) over EncryptedValue for encryption. It introduces CMP version 3 to signal support for the new encryption format. It adds extended key usages to identify CMP roles, new general message types for requesting CA certificates and CRL updates, and well-known URI paths for HTTP-based CMP.
tldr.outcome: CMP deployments can now use modern cryptographic structures with better crypto agility and clearer role delegation. However, this RFC was replaced by RFC 9810 and 9811, which combine these updates into consolidated specifications for CMP and HTTP-based CMP.

today: RFC 9480 was a Standards Track update published in November 2023, but it is now superseded by RFC 9810 and RFC 9811, which consolidate its updates into complete CMP specifications.

sections.title: CMP and Why It Needs Updating
sections.content:
Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) is a protocol for automated certificate enrollment, renewal, and revocation. It was originally defined in RFC 4210 (published in 1999 as RFC 2510). CMP is used by enterprises and IoT systems to manage large numbers of device certificates.

Real-world deployments revealed limitations in CMP version 2. The protocol used EncryptedValue, a structure that has been deprecated in favor of EnvelopedData as defined in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) standard. Additionally, CMP lacked a formal way to express role-based authorization (distinguishing a Certification Authority from a Registration Authority), limiting its flexibility for delegated certificate management. This RFC addresses these and other issues identified during implementations of CMP in industrial and IoT environments.
sections.eli5: CMP is a system for automatically handing out and updating digital certificates. The original design is old and uses encryption methods that are no longer preferred. This update brings it into the modern era.

sections.title: Core Changes: EnvelopedData and Version 3
sections.content:
The most significant change is replacing EncryptedValue with EnvelopedData as the preferred encryption structure. EnvelopedData, defined in CMS (RFC 5652), is a standardized approach used across many cryptographic protocols. It supports three key management techniques: key transport (protecting the encryption key with the recipient's public key), key agreement (using Diffie-Hellman or similar), and password-based encryption (using a shared secret). This provides flexibility for different deployment scenarios.

CMP version 2 messages can still use the old EncryptedValue for backward compatibility, but CMP version 3 signals explicit support for EnvelopedData. Version 3 also enables the use of explicit hash algorithm identifiers in certificate confirmation messages, which is important for preparing for post-quantum signature algorithms that may not have a direct hash algorithm encoding.

The EncryptedKey structure now offers a choice: implementations can use either the deprecated EncryptedValue or the newer EnvelopedData. This design preserves backward compatibility while allowing new deployments to adopt the more modern approach.
sections.eli5: The protocol switches to a standard encryption method used everywhere else in cryptography. A new version number (3) tells both sides that this modern method is supported. Old messages can still work the old way.

sections.title: Extended Key Usages and Roles
sections.content:
CMP introduces three extended key usages (EKUs) to formally identify and authorize different PKI management roles. These allow a Certification Authority to delegate specific functions to other entities while proving that delegation through the certificate itself.

id-kp-cmcCA identifies a Certification Authority authorized to issue certificates. id-kp-cmcRA identifies a Registration Authority delegated to perform authorization checks and manage certificate requests on behalf of the CA. id-kp-cmKGA identifies a Key Generation Authority authorized to generate key pairs on behalf of end entities, a sensitive operation that requires explicit authorization.

These EKUs appear in the certificate used to sign or authenticate CMP messages. An implementation can validate the authorization of a CMP peer by checking that its certificate contains the appropriate EKU. This eliminates the need for out-of-band configuration to express delegation and enables automated authorization checks.
sections.eli5: The protocol now has official badges that say 'I am allowed to issue certificates' or 'I am allowed to generate keys on your behalf.' These badges are in the certificate itself, so everyone knows who is allowed to do what.

sections.title: New General Message Types
sections.content:
RFC 9480 adds new general message types that endpoints can request from a CMP server using the genm (general message) mechanism. These include requests for CA certificates, root CA certificate updates, certificate request templates, and CRL updates. Previously, CMP lacked a standardized way to request these common certificate management operations.

The document also extends the polling mechanism (originally designed for long-running requests) to work with several additional message types: p10cr (PKCS #10 certificate requests), certConf (certificate confirmation), rr (revocation requests), genm (general messages), and error messages. This allows clients and servers to poll for the result of ongoing operations across a wider range of message types.

A new certProfile field in the PKIHeader allows endpoints to indicate specific certificate profiles when requesting certificates. This is useful when a CA supports multiple profiles and the client needs to specify which one to use.
sections.eli5: The protocol adds new standardized requests: 'give me your CA certificate,' 'send me a template for certificate requests,' and 'send me the CRL update.' Polling (asking 'is it ready yet?') now works on more types of requests.

sections.title: HTTP Transfer and Well-Known URIs
sections.content:
RFC 9480 updates RFC 6712, which specifies how to carry CMP messages over HTTP. The primary change introduces well-known URI path segments for CMP operations. Instead of requiring out-of-band configuration of specific HTTP paths for different message types, implementations can use standardized paths like /.well-known/cmp followed by the operation type.

This simplification reduces configuration complexity and makes it easier for CMP clients to discover and use CMP servers. A server implementing CMP over HTTP can now advertise a single base URI, and clients automatically derive the correct path for specific operations.

The document also clarifies the HTTP request-URI format and how different CMP messages map to HTTP endpoints, improving interoperability between CMP implementations that use HTTP transport.
sections.eli5: When CMP runs over the web, it now uses standard web addresses like '/.well-known/cmp' so both sides know exactly where to find each other without needing a manual setup guide.
